doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Wardell Gray's death and the mixed casino in Las Vegas
summary: Benny Carter's band opens a casino for minorities in Vegas in 1955; Gray is found dead in the desert.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: No he couldn’t do it. But anyhow then Wardell, in 1955 Wardell, he was with the Benny Carter band. And the Benny Carter band, they opened up this mixed casino in Las Vegas. First time they’d ever had anything like that. It was — I’ve forgotten what they call it. Maybe it was The Flamingo, I can’t remember. But it was a casino down there that catered to minorities. Because Vegas you know, it was very segregated. Strictly segregated. When Basie when there the guys had to come in the back door.
And this is why he opened this?

In 1955. In the middle of the year. So Benny Carter had the band there and one of our musicians here, Alan Smith, a very fine trumpet player who lives here, he was in the band. So they went down there and they opened up. Opening night after the gig they found Wardell out in the desert dead. So they don’t know whether it was a drug deal gone awry or — to this day nobody knows what happened. But that just has to do with Wardell Gray. And by that time I was working with Bob Scobey. And we were in Chicago at the Blue Note. Now the Blue Note was quite famous in its day. They had 750 seating capacity and everybody played there: Basie, Kenton, everybody played here. And they brought Bob Scobey’s band in in 1955. We went in in 1954 in October just for a two week engagement and opened — Sundays and Thursdays were off nights — so we opened on a Monday night, nobody; Tuesday night, nobody; Wednesday night, nobody. Friday night people were lined up around the block. And the first two or three days the girls, all the cocktail waitresses, they were grumbling you know.
